quests.explanation: From Latin 'lex' (law) and 'lation' (carrying), legislation is literally the process of 'carrying' new laws into effect.
From Latin 'jus' (law) and 'dicere' (to speak), jurisdiction describes the legal authority to 'speak' or rule on a matter.
Dropping the final 'e' before adding '-ion' is the same familiar pattern; litigation describes the formal process of taking legal action.
From Latin 'arbiter' (judge), arbitration describes settling a dispute through a neutral third party rather than a full court case.
When a verb ends in '-y' after a consonant, the noun form often changes 'y' to 'i' before adding '-ance,' as in 'comply' to 'compliance.'
The suffix '-ory' turns the verb 'regulate' into an adjective describing anything related to creating or enforcing rules.
This compound word describes someone who 'holds' a 'share' (portion of ownership) in a company.
Sharing a root with 'divide,' a dividend is a portion of company profit 'divided' among shareholders.
From Italian 'portafoglio' (a case for carrying papers), 'portfolio' now describes a collection of investments, designs, or work samples.
From Latin 'mort' (death), amortization describes gradually 'killing off' a debt through scheduled payments over time.
From Greek 'pro-' (before) and 'gnosis' (knowledge), a prognosis is a doctor's prediction made 'before' knowing the final outcome.
From Greek 'an-' (without) and 'aisthesis' (sensation), anesthesia literally means 'without sensation.'
From Latin 'convalescere' (to grow strong), convalescence describes the period of recovering strength after an illness.
From Greek 'epi-' (upon) and 'demos' (people), an epidemic is a disease spreading 'upon' (among) a population.
From Latin 'vacca' (cow), 'vaccination' is named after the first vaccine, made from cowpox — the double 'c' comes directly from that root.
This compound word describes a 'patient' treated without staying overnight — they go 'out' the same day.
The prefix 'para-' means 'alongside,' so a paramedic works 'alongside' doctors, providing emergency care before hospital arrival.
This technical compound word describes software that sits in the 'middle,' connecting other programs together.
The suffix '-ization' turns the adjective 'virtual' into a noun describing the process of creating a simulated version of something.
When an adjective ends in '-able,' the noun form changes to '-ability,' as in 'scalable' to 'scalability.'
Related to 'consul' (a government representative), a consulate is the official office where that representative works abroad.
From Latin 'ex-' (out of) and 'patria' (homeland), an expatriate is literally someone living 'out of' their home country.
The suffix '-ary' turns the noun 'custom' into an adjective describing something done as a regular practice.
From Greek 'nomas' (wandering), 'nomadic' describes a lifestyle of moving from place to place rather than settling permanently.
Simply add '-ing' to the compound noun-turned-verb 'backpack,' describing budget travel carrying your belongings on your back.

quests.hint: Tricky letters: OD-YS-SEY, a name turned common noun.
quests.explanation: Named after Homer's epic 'The Odyssey,' this word now describes any long, eventful journey.
The suffix '-age' turns 'pilgrim' (a traveler on a religious journey) into the noun describing that journey itself.
From 'Sabbath' (a day of rest), a sabbatical is an extended break, often from work, originally modeled on a yearly rest period.
Borrowed from German, this compound word literally means a strong 'desire' (lust) to 'wander' and explore.
This vivid compound word describes someone who 'trots' (travels briskly) all around the 'globe.'
